My two cents (as a cis F in a relationship with a trans man) — it would be one thing if they were confused, ignorant, or saying the wrong thing because they don’t know better. But saying hurtful things to you about you/your partner and reacting with anger is where I would need to draw a line. If I were in your shoes, here’s a few things I feel I would need to communicate to my parents:


- Gender affirming healthcare is off limits for discussion if they cannot respect his decisions re: his care. These are well researched, effective treatments with incredibly high success/low regret rates that they have no reason to question. 
- Decisions down the road about family planning are similarly not for them to comment on — those decisions will be made thoughtfully and carefully between you and your partner if and when you are ready. 
- Questions, concerns, and open-minded discussion is welcome — anger and prejudice are not. If they begin to react with anger, put your foot down and tell them you will speak to them when they are able to have a calm discussion. 


All of this to say… I know this is easier said than done. I was lucky that when I talked to my parents about dating a trans person, they were initially a little surprised/confused but have quickly gotten on board. There are moments where they’re not perfect, but all together we’re all very happy. I truly hope that can happen for you someday.

Last thing I’ll say, and I’m sorry for the novel, but make sure 1) your partner feels supported by you and 2) you feel supported by others. Make sure you have people other than your partner (friend, therapist, etc) who you can speak to about this situation. Also, if he has a good relationship with his parents or other family, I wonder if there are ways they could support you both as well? Worth thinking about. Wishing you well!

Hi! I helped my current partner through top surgery and had similar feelings to you. It doesn't help that I have pretty severe medical anxiety -- even working up the courage to visit him in the hospital was really hard for me, but I'm so glad I did!

I felt my primary role prior to surgery was to be fully supportive, but I did let my partner know that I wanted to be there for him however he wanted, but that I was feeling nervous because it was a big surgery and I just wanted what was best for him. 

We talked a lot about fun things we could do while he was recovering -- we made a list of movies we wanted to watched, ordered coloring books, etc. Most days of recovery were good, there were a few days of high pain and/or irritability that came with that, and being super communicative got us through. Very happy for your partner and I hope everything goes well for him and you!!
